newsitem.title: UK: Princess Diana makes mark on international stage.
newsitem.headline: Princess Diana makes mark on international stage.

text.p: Princess Diana was due back in Britain on Thursday after a controversial Angolan tour dominated by the issue of landmines, firm in the knowledge that she has established herself as a powerful player on the world stage.

During her four days in the southern African nation, Diana donned khakis and a flak jacket, toured a minefield, comforted amputees and called for a worldwide ban on the "hideous weapons" -- comments that caused a political storm back home.

In just a few days, the princess did more for the eradication of landmines than countless international meetings and in the process proved she is far more than just the attractive ex-wife of a future king.

"As soon as Diana, Princess of Wales decided to go to Angola to look at land mines, I knew that this would be The Big Issue of 1997. Such is the power of the princess," columnist Barbara Amiel wrote in The Daily Telegraph.
Foreign ministers from 50 countries are due in Ottawa in October to discuss the 1980 convention to ban landmines.

"With the princess's words echoing in their ears, and a few well placed placards showing her alongside Angola's injured victims, who can doubt that the atmosphere will be transformed?" asked The Times newspaper.
The Red Cross also heaped praise on the princess.

"At the British Red Cross we are delighted that the visit by Diana, Princess of Wales, to Angola has helped enormously to raise awareness of the effects of anti-personnel mines," John Grey, director of public affairs, told Reuters.
"We hope this awareness will encourage international communities to ban the use of mines."

"The simple act of speaking from the heart, speaking as a mother and drawing attention to the impact of such devices, is done better by Princess Diana than anyone else anywhere," said journalist Mary Kenny in The Express newspaper.

After months out of the headlines or just pictured in designer gowns at charity galas, Diana is back where she claims she has always wanted to be: helping people in her self-declared role as Britain's roving ambassador or "Queen of Hearts."

The princess defended her controversial comments, which seemed to contradict government policy on landmines and were read by some ruling Conservatives as an endorsement for the opposition Labour Party, tipped to win the next election.
"All I am trying to do is to help...That is all I'm trying to do," Diana told journalists in the town of Kuito.

Her visit, on behalf of the Red Cross to highlight the problem of landmines, had been sanctioned by the government. The princess had been fully briefed and had not been expected to butt heads with the government on the issue.
One junior minister branded Diana a "loose cannon" and called her views on landmines "ill-advised" and "not helpful".

Defence Minister Michael Portillo quickly played down the row, however, dismissing the row as a misunderstanding. The junior minister who admitted speaking to journalists about Diana said later he had "the greatest admiration for her work."
Diana, meanwhile, was finishing up her humanitarian work and had little time for the political squabbling at home.
"This is a distraction we did not need," Diana said about the furore brewing in Britain, proving that she is determined to speak her mind about the causes she believes in.
Whether this is just the first of many international forays for good causes remains to be seen but Diana has shown that she is a force to be reckoned with.
The Times, in an editorial, said some people may even be having second thoughts about stripping Diana of her royal title, which she lost on her divorce from Prince Charles.

"Neither Buckingham Palace nor Downing Street may have fully apppreciated that when she lost her status as Royal Highness she gained a freedom to speak out on issues that were previously forbidden territory. She now has a licence to provoke, and she gives every sign of being willing to use it," it said.
